catalog_quote: In EA stress is not a major problem, as its occurrence is almost totally predictable in terms of syllable structure. As in English, a word never has more than one primary, or heavy, stress; and long vowels never occur unstressed. Remember that EA does not permit more than one long vowel in a word; in case of two long vowels (resulting from morphological suffixation), the first gets shortened and the stress shifts to the second long vowel ... sweep_summary: Egyptian (Cairene) Arabic is in the catalog as weight-sensitive on Abdel-Massih 1975. Of 13 title hits, 9 are about Cairene word stress, 3 are intonation/discourse prosody (Hellmuth 2006 x2, Hellmuth 2007, Ward & Al Bayyari 2007) and one is a general theory (Hagberg). Two were obtained open and read: Welden 1980 'Stress in Cairo Arabic' (SLS 10(2), whole volume on archive.org; IDEALS hdl 2142/9324) and Hagberg 2006 (SIL e-Book 3, via Internet Archive copy of the SIL PDF). Welden gives a first-hand, informant-tested rule (p. 102) that confirms every clause of the catalog's rule (penult default; final CVCC/CVV(C); LLL antepenult; final CVC light; katabítu penult) and refines it (alternating count for all-light strings, unstressed long vowels shorten, proclitics outside the domain, secondary rhythmic stress exists, p. 111); it is a better deciding source than the textbook and should replace or head the citation, with the 'weight' coding unchanged. Hagberg reproduces Hayes' 1991 Cairene rule (p. 7) second-hand, consistent with both. Aquil 2014's abstract (Crossref) states primary stress is uncontroversially on one of the last three syllables and argues secondary stress exists (refines the catalog's 'no secondary stress' note). Not obtainable by automated download: McCarthy 1979 LI (JSTOR; UMass ScholarWorks 403), Welden 1977 UT Austin diss., Guindy 1988 ZAL, Harms 1981 Linguistic Analysis, Larudee 1973 Language Sciences, Hayes 1995 (Google Books preview only), Hellmuth 2006/2007 (SOAS eprints unreachable; De Gruyter paywalled).org, IDEALS, MPI PuRe and the the Internet Archive.

new_statements.quote: In order to avoid the multiplication of diacritic signs, the sign for accent (') has been employed as sparingly as possible. This sign is placed at the beginning of the syllable accented; e.g. (below) ka'man (accent on second syllable), 'fahma (on first syllable). If the following two points are remembered, they will be found a sufficient guide to almost all the words which have no accent-mark: (1) a long vowel (: or ·) is invariably the accented vowel; (2) if there is no long vowel, the accent is on the last syllable but one, unless otherwise marked.

new_statements.relation_note: Same type as the catalog and Welden 1980: right-edge, weight-sensitive, CVV always stressed, penult by default, long vowels shorten when unstressed, clitics shift the accent. It is a coarser pedagogical statement: it does not spell out the CVC-heavy-penult vs antepenult condition, the superheavy-ultima clause, or the even/odd light-string pattern (katabítu); those cases are handled by explicit accent marks in the text. Nothing in it contradicts the catalog. Describes the Cairo colloquial (School of Oriental Studies, Cairo; footnotes on the Alphabet page note Upper Egyptian pronunciation differences).
new_statements.rule_in_words: A practical rule for the learner: the syllable with the long (or half-long) vowel always carries the accent; if the word has no long vowel the accent falls on the penult; anything else is marked with the accent sign in the text (e.g. ka'man with final-syllable accent, the shortened reflex of kamaan). Vowel length in the notation is phonemic, so this is a weight-sensitive system in which CVV attracts the accent and the default is the penult.
new_statements.secondary_stress: p. 137, footnote 1: 'Where more than one accent appears to fall on a single word-group, it will be found that the last is the strongest, and the rest secondary.' (about clitic groups such as verb + object + dative suffixes); nothing on rhythmic secondary stress inside simple words.
new_statements.exceptions: 'unless otherwise marked': words not covered by the two points carry an explicit accent sign. Suffix pronouns 'never receive accent by themselves' (p. 27) and a suffix 'throws accent on to the preceding syllable, as suffixes do' (p. 85, on dative l-+pronoun, e.g. lak); repeated notes on 'shifting of accent' with vowel elision and loss of length under suffixation and annexation (pp. 35, 45, 51, 75, 81, 129, 137); long vowels shorten when they lose the accent (p. 129: ji'bi:Su 'they sell' but jibi'Su:ha). Fuller rules are referred to the companion volume 'The Phonetics of Arabic' (pp. 68-72).
new_statements.identity_note: Both readable works describe Cairo/Lower Egyptian colloquial: Gairdner is a Cairo (School of Oriental Studies) conversation grammar whose Alphabet page footnotes note Upper Egyptian pronunciation differences; McCarthy's section is explicitly about 'a dialect spoken in Egypt from Cairo northward' and contrasts it with Damascene and with Classical Arabic as read by Cairenes.

[p. 105:] (4) a. Stress a superheavy ultima. b. Otherwise stress a heavy penult. c. new_statements.rule_in_words: Cairene: a superheavy final syllable (CVVC, CVCC) is stressed; otherwise a heavy penult (CVC, CVV) is stressed; otherwise the penult or antepenult is stressed according to parity, counting light syllables in pairs from the left edge of the word or from the rightmost non-final heavy syllable (búxala, katabítu, ?inkásara, muxtálifa). A word-final CVC counts as light (mudárris, ?ábadan); heavy antepenults reject stress (martába, yiktíbu). Formalised as binary left-to-right feet over pairs of light syllables with a right-branching word tree (p. 106).
new_statements.secondary_stress: No explicit statement about Cairene secondary stress in the Cairene section; the left-to-right binary feet imply rhythmic structure but McCarthy does not spell out secondary prominence for Arabic. Section 3.6 'Secondary Stress' (p. 180 ff.) concerns Tiberian Hebrew.
new_statements.exceptions: Final CVV is always stressed in colloquial words (ramáa 'he threw him', ?axúu) but is analysed as an underlying superheavy CVVh with suffixal h deleted (pp. 114-116); in Classical Arabic words read by Cairenes a final CVV is unstressed. Morphological exception: 3 f. sg. verb suffix -it plus an object clitic takes the stress (kallimítak, ramítu, expected *kallímitak, *rámitu; pp. 116-118), handled by a 'Feminine Adjunction' rule. Harrell's rule fails for long light strings in Classical words read by Cairenes (baqarátuhu, sajarátuhu, p. 105), which the parity rule (4c) covers.

sources.quote: Each EA word has one primary ( i.e., relatively more prominent ) stress. The domain of primary stress is almost totally predictable in terms of syllable structure. Primary stress is most frequently on the penult ( i.e., pre-final syllable ), e.g., yiktibu 'they write', madrasa 'school'. However, in certain cases, primary stress occurs on the ultima ( i.e., the final syllable ), and in other cases it occurs on the antepenult ( i.e., the third syllable from the end ). The ultima is stressed if (a) it contains a long vowel or if (b) it ends in two consonants, e.g., katabuu 'they wrote it', katabt 'I wrote'. The antepenult is stressed if the last three syllables have the structure CVCVCV(C), e.g., sabaka 'a net', katabit 'she wrote', inkasarit 'it broke', muxtalifa 'different (fs)'. Contrary to the above rules, primary stress is on the penult if the structure CVCVCV(C) constitutes a feminine singular perfect-tense verb whose final V(C) is a pronoun suffix, e.g., ramitu 'she threw it away'. Again, primary stress is usually on the penult if the structure CVCVCV constitutes a broken plural form with identical high vowels in the first two syllables, e.g., sibita 'baskets', numura 'tigers'.

sources.quote: The Cairene dialect of Arabic shows quantity-sensitive trochaic parsing (CVC and CVː are heavy) with a prohibition on final stress except when the final syllable is superheavy (CVCC or CVːC). When the final syllable is not superheavy, the stress pattern is as follows: stress the penult if it is heavy, as in (18a), but when the penult is light, stress either the penult (18b) or the antepenult (18c), whichever is an even number of syllables away from the rightmost non-final heavy syllable or the beginning of the word.

sources.quote: In the literature, pre-generative (Harrell, 1960; Mitchell, 1960), generative (Hayes, 1995; Watson, 2002), and typological accounts (Hulst van der and Hellmuth, 2010) exist, which all identify Cairene Arabic as a quantity-sensitive language in which the parsing of syllables into feet is sensitive to syllabic weight: a super-heavy final syllable with long vowels followed by a consonant (CVVC) receives main stress, otherwise a heavy penult with a long vowel or a short vowel followed by a consonant is stressed or a light antepenult in words ending in three light syllables (open syllables with short vowels). According to McCarthy (1979), bimoraic trochees consisting of either one heavy syllable or two light syllables are built in a left to right manner.
